The Prophet

Kahlil Gibran's influential 1923 book, 'The Prophet', is a seminal work of prose poetry that has had a lasting impact on modern literature and culture. This Lebanese-American poet and writer drew upon his experiences living in the United States and his exploration of Eastern mysticism to create a collection of 26 short fables that have been translated into over 40 languages.

Through its vivid imagery, metaphors, and exploration of universal themes such as love, freedom, and the human condition, 'The Prophet' has resonated with readers across cultures and time zones. Gibran's innovative style and his emphasis on the importance of individualism, spirituality, and self-discovery have made him one of the most beloved and respected writers of the 20th century.

Gibran's work has also been influential in shaping modern art, music, and film, with its themes and imagery continuing to inspire artists and audiences today.





The Prophet was first published in 1923 by Alfred A. Knopf and went on to become a bestseller, selling over 20 million copies worldwide. It has been translated into many languages and remains one of the most widely read and influential books of the 20th century.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Prophet is a collection of 26 poetic essays (or prose poems) by the Lebanese-American poet, artist, and philosopher Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931), first published in English by Alfred A. Knopf in New York on 23 September 1923. The book presents the wisdom teachings of a prophetic figure named Almustafa ('the chosen and the beloved'), who, on the day of his departure from the city of Orphalese after twelve years, is asked by the people to speak on the great themes of human life — Love, Marriage, Children, Work, Joy and Sorrow, Houses, Clothes, Buying and Selling, Crime and Punishment, Laws, Freedom, Reason and Passion, Pain, Self-Knowledge, Teaching, Friendship, Talking, Time, Good and Evil, Prayer, Pleasure, Beauty, Religion, and Death.

The Prophet is the best-selling book ever published by Alfred A. Knopf and one of the best-selling books of the 20th century — it remained in print continuously from its first publication, was translated into over 100 languages, and sold over 100 million copies worldwide by the end of the 20th century. It achieved its greatest cultural impact during the counter-culture movement of the 1960s–1970s, when its themes of spiritual freedom, universal love, and transcendence of social convention resonated with the counter-culture's rejection of conventional religion and politics. Passages from The Prophet are regularly read at weddings, funerals, and religious ceremonies, and its aphoristic style has made it one of the most widely quoted books of the 20th century.

Gibran's prose style — biblical in its rhythms, Sufi in its imagery, and Transcendentalist in its philosophical temper — synthesises Arabic literary tradition (Arabic poetry, Islamic mysticism), Blake's prophetic books, Nietzsche's Zarathustra, and American Transcendentalism (Emerson, Whitman) into a distinctively accessible mystical idiom. The Prophet

A 20th-century writer and poet, Kahlil Gibran, created a seminal work called The Prophet, which brought together elements of mysticism, spirituality, and social commentary.

Published in 1923, this influential book features 26 prose poetry fables that have resonated with readers worldwide for generations. Gibran's unique blend of philosophical introspection and poetic language has made The Prophet a timeless classic, inspiring countless adaptations, interpretations, and translations across cultures.

The work's impact extends beyond its literary significance to encompass social and cultural implications, as it encourages readers to question conventional norms and embrace individuality.

In the realm of spirituality, Gibran's ideas have been seen as a bridge between Eastern mysticism and Western philosophy, offering a profound perspective on human existence and our place in the world.

Gibran's legacy is intertwined with broader historical trends, including the rise of modernism and the emergence of new spiritual movements. As such, The Prophet stands as a testament to the enduring power of literature to shape our understanding of ourselves and our shared human experiences.
